centres.opened: Built 1928 and opened as a wet market (Maxwell Market, also called Kim Hua Market) in 1929 per Roots; Wikipedia gives an opening date of 17 November 1928. Converted to a food centre in 1987 and renamed Maxwell Food Centre in 2001 after renovation. NEA's dataset lists 1935.

look.summary: A low, open-sided food pavilion made of linked single-storey sheds with sloping tan roofs and peach and orange gable ends, set among big shade trees at the edge of Chinatown with office towers rising behind. Inside, long aisles of stalls with lit signboards face rows of fixed tables, and the sides stay open to the street and the breeze.

knownFor.note: Tian Tian Hainanese Chicken Rice holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand and became world famous after Anthony Bourdain called it his favourite place for the dish.

Pang Siew Ting began frying Fuzhou oyster cakes in the 1960s, and her children now run Maxwell Fuzhou Oyster Cake, which the Michelin Guide lists; each cake is fried to order with oysters, prawns and minced pork in a crisp shell.
Zhen Zhen Porridge at Maxwell is featured in the Michelin Guide's list of places for comforting congee, with fish, pork and century egg versions.

knownFor.dish: Ngoh hiang (five-spice meat rolls and fritters)
knownFor.note: China Street Fritters began as a street stall in 1942, moved into Maxwell in 1987 and made its ngoh hiang by hand until it closed there in 2022 for lack of a successor (it later reopened in Telok Blangah).
Wikipedia lists ham chim peng among Maxwell's well-known foods; a long-running ham chim peng stall here reportedly closed after about 40 years.

history.fact: The land was a Chinese burial ground cleared in 1907, and the market building was finished in 1928 and opened for trade in 1929.
Soon after opening it lost trade to street hawkers, so cooked food stalls and eating tables were added around 1929 to 1930.
From December 1946 the market housed the first of the Social Welfare Department's 'Family Restaurants', which sold cheap meals at eight cents to poor and displaced residents.
In 1986 about 70 street hawkers from China Square were moved in to join 22 cooked food stalls already there, and in 1987 the market was formally converted into a food centre.

centres.opened: Built in 1981 as the Kreta Ayer Complex (Roots, NEA); the last Chinatown street hawkers moved in during October 1983; renamed Chinatown Complex in 1984. NEA's dataset lists 1983.

The food centre fills the whole second floor: a dense grid of hundreds of stalls with green and white tiled pillars, big wall fans, red paper lanterns and glowing menu boards.

Lian He Ben Ji Claypot has cooked each pot over charcoal since 1979 and is a Michelin Bib Gourmand awardee.
Ann Chin Popiah, founded in the 1940s, makes its thin skins by hand and was given a Michelin Plate in 2019.

history.fact: The complex was built in 1981 during Chinatown's urban renewal to house the area's remaining street hawkers.
In October 1983 about 300 street hawkers from the surrounding streets moved into the newly finished $18 million complex.
Its designers added Chinese touches such as pavilions, arches, clay tiles and pitched roofs so the block would fit the look of old Chinatown.
After a major renovation it reopened in 2008 with more than 700 stalls.

Lao Fu Zi Fried Kway Teow appears on the Michelin Bib Gourmand lists for 2019 and 2021.

knownFor.note: To-Ricos Guo Shi was a new Bib Gourmand entry in 2019 for its flat rice noodles with pork belly, intestine and tofu braised in spiced soy.
Xin Mei Xiang Zheng Zong Lor Mee is a well-known stall here that often sells out early, serving noodles in thick, vinegary braising gravy with fish and braised pork.
Toa Payoh Rojak is often recommended here for its mix of fruit, vegetables and dough fritters in prawn paste and tamarind dressing with crushed peanuts.

history.fact: The centre was built to give permanent space to street hawkers around Kallang Airport Estate, a housing estate laid out on the runway of the old Kallang Airport after the airport closed in 1955.
In 1973 a stall here, Khoon Kee Chicken Rice, won Singapore's first competition for the cleanest cooked food stall, sponsored by the Rotary Club.
A 5.8 million dollar upgrade in 2006 to 2007, the largest of NEA's Hawker Centre Upgrading Programme at the time, raised seating to about 1,904.
The centre closed from June to September 2024 for repairs and reopened on 1 October 2024 with new tables and stools, high-speed fans, refurbished toilets and fresh paint.

545 Whampoa Prawn Noodles, run by a third-generation hawker, appears in the Michelin Guide and serves noodles with prawns, pork and a rich prawn broth.
Lonely Planet singles out Ar Rahman Royal Prata here for murtabak, the stuffed savoury pancake.
Thin lentil and rice pancakes are among the South Indian staples visitors queue for here.
Stalls serve vegetarian meals on banana leaves or stainless steel platters alongside North Indian, Malay and Chinese vegetarian food.
Pulled milk tea is a standard order alongside biryani and prata at Tekka.

history.fact: The first market here, Kandang Kerbau Market, opened in 1915 with a colonial-style building of arches and ornate steelwork designed by Municipal Engineer Robert Peirce.

The new complex first carried the name Buffalo Road Market and Cooked Food Centre, was renamed Zhujiao Centre in November 1981 under the push to use Hanyu Pinyin names, and became Tekka Centre in 2000 after residents objected.
The name Tekka comes from the Hokkien for 'foot of the small bamboos', after bamboo that once grew along the Rochor Canal.
The centre closed for upgrading in 2008 and reopened in 2009, then shut again from July to October 2023 for repairs that added a purple paint scheme, bigger fans and bird netting.

Hup Kee Fried Oyster Omelette, which began as a street stall about 50 years ago, holds a Bib Gourmand, and in 1978 a Newton oyster omelette stall was picked by the tourism board for its Rasa Singapura food centre.
Satay and sambal stingray with beer are what the characters eat in the Crazy Rich Asians hawker scene filmed here.
Heng, a Bib Gourmand stall run by an owner with over 50 years of experience, fries both the white (egg) and black (sweet soy) versions.

knownFor.note: Michelin lists black pepper crab among the classics sold in Newton's rows of stalls, and Alliance Seafood offers sambal, black pepper or salted egg yolk sauces.

history.fact: Street hawkers gathered at the Newton crossroads from the 1950s, and a weekly bazaar there became so popular that by 1960 it ran three nights a week.
When it opened in 1971 it was Singapore's first hawker centre built without a wet market, laid out as hawker stalls in a garden setting to suit the garden city image.
It was built to take in street hawkers moved off Koek Road and the Orchard Road car park, the night food spot known as Glutton's Square.
A 1982 survey found it was the second most popular eating place in Singapore with 7,309 daily patrons; it was rebuilt from 2005 and reopened on 1 July 2006.

Sweet grilled wings from stalls such as Good Luck Chicken Wings and Satay are a standard order here.

knownFor.note: Time Out singles out the carrot cake at stall 36 and the fried oyster at Ang Sa Lee.
Drinks stalls sell sugarcane juice in giant mugs and three litre towers to go with the barbecue.

history.fact: The English name Chomp Chomp is an adaptation of the older Teochew name Tiong Tiong, meaning loyalty and righteousness.
It opened in May 1972 at a cost of $95,000 with 36 built in stalls, each with its own sink and neon light, to take in hawkers from the street eating spot on Kensington Park Road.
Stallholders went from renting to owning their stalls under the Stall Ownership Scheme in 1996, and a roof over the seating was finished in 1998.
It was voted Singaporeans' favourite hawker centre in the City Hawker Food Hunt between 2011 and 2013.

centres.opened: Seng Poh Road Market completed in 1950 and officially opened in 1951 (Roots, NEA); temporary market sheds on the area dated from 1940 (Roots). Wikipedia's Tiong Bahru article instead gives 1945 for the first wet market and 1955 for a larger market. Renamed Tiong Bahru Market in 1993; rebuilt 2004 to 2006. NEA's dataset lists the year as unknown.

look.summary: A two-storey market with rounded Art Deco corners painted white with bold red bands, a tall red drum at the entrance carrying Chinese characters, and a curved dark canopy above, wrapped around a central garden courtyard. The food centre upstairs is a wide, bright hall with pale green columns banded in blue, a white ceiling with round recessed coves, and a railed opening that looks down into the courtyard and its palms.

Tiong Bahru Hainanese Boneless Chicken Rice has served here since 1988 and is a Bib Gourmand recipient.
178 Lor Mee is one of the market's best-known stalls, with waits of 20 minutes or more.
Hong Heng Fried Sotong Prawn Mee is a third-generation stall with a Bib Gourmand since 2016.
Koh Brother Pig's Organ Soup is a family stall dating to 1955 and a Bib Gourmand awardee.

history.fact: Before the permanent market, traders used a row of temporary sheds put up in 1940, which were too small by the late 1940s.
Work on a new market began in 1950 and it opened in 1951 under the name Seng Poh Road Market, serving residents of the new Tiong Bahru flats.
After a full revamp in 1993 it was renamed Tiong Bahru Market.
Between 2004 and 2006 the old market was closed and replaced with a new building that borrows Art Deco touches from the surrounding estate.

knownFor.note: A Noodle Story won a Bib Gourmand in 2017 and caps itself at 200 bowls a day, so it often sells out by about 1:45pm at lunch.
Hoo Kee Bak Chang is on the 2025 Michelin Bib Gourmand list for its glutinous rice dumplings.
J2 Famous Crispy Curry Puff sells curry and sardine puffs and is on the 2025 Bib Gourmand list.
Quan Ji, a zi char stall here, was featured in the Michelin Guide in 2018.

history.fact: The Housing and Development Board began building the centre in 1982 at a cost of about S$5.83 million, and it opened in April 1983.
It was built to serve office workers and to take in street hawkers from Stanley Street, Boon Tat Street, Cecil Street, Amoy Street and Telok Ayer Street.
It closed in September 2002 for a S$2.8 million upgrade and reopened in March 2003.

history.fact: Hong Lim Market and Food Centre was built in 1978, making it one of the first proper hawker centres in Chinatown, earlier than nearby Amoy Street and Maxwell food centres.
It was built to give shelter to roving hawkers who once lined Nankin Street, Hokkien Street and Sua Kia Teng near North Canal Road.
It sits inside Hong Lim Complex, an HDB development on Upper Cross Street that mixes shops and a food centre below with flats above.
A major upgrade in May 2011 improved ventilation and added seats, and the centre now has more than 100 cooked food stalls.

NHB pairs mutton soup with nasi lemak as the centre's signature, and Bahrakath Mutton Soup, selling since 1973, won a Bib Gourmand in 2023.
Adam Road Noo Cheng Big Prawn Noodle, running for over three decades, won a Bib Gourmand in 2023.
Adam's Indian Rojak is listed among the centre's popular stalls.

history.fact: The Public Works Department set up 32 temporary food stalls beside the Bukit Timah Canal in 1971, and road building plans led to the new centre that opened on 28 September 1974.
In the 1980s it was a regular lunch stop for police on patrol, students from nearby schools and hired drivers.
Its 2002 upgrade cost $1.73 million, raised the floor against flooding from the nearby canal, and kept the nine sided plan and five old angsana trees.

history.fact: A makeshift hawker shelter stood at the entrance to Kampong Geylang Serai before 1930, long before the market building.
The first Geylang Serai Market opened in 1964, and by 1975 its eating house was noted for having Singapore's largest variety of Muslim food.
The market was rebuilt between 2006 and 2009 in the shape of a Malay kampung house, with a raised ceiling for natural ventilation and light.
The Hari Raya light-up in Geylang Serai began in 1985 and runs alongside the yearly Ramadan bazaar.

history.fact: It was built on reclaimed land and opened in 1978 to serve the beach front of what was then Singapore's largest seaside resort.
Its first hawkers came from Alkaff Lane, and in the 1980s sales were poor even though it was Singapore's only seaside hawker centre.
It was renamed East Coast Lagoon Food Centre in 1981 and Food Rendezvous in 1992, then rebuilt in a Balinese resort style for $4.5 million and reopened as the Food Village in January 2004.
A fire hit four stalls in June 2013, and the centre closed for three months for a $1.5 million upgrade; it was upgraded again from November 2020 to February 2021.

history.fact: Golden Mile Food Centre was completed in 1975 to house hawkers resettled from the Jalan Sultan street market.
Its upper floor became known as the Army Market because the area was close to the headquarters of uniformed groups and the Beach Road Camp, so military supply shops gathered there.
After a six-month closure in 2002, the centre closed again from December 2020 to March 2021 so its ventilators and fans could be replaced.

history.fact: Changi Village grew up beside British military camps from 1927, and after most British servicemen left by 1971 it became a struggling kampong.
A government plan to renew the area began in 1973, and the hawker centre was completed in 1975.
In the 1980s the centre was packed at lunch with soldiers, air force personnel, and airport and industrial estate workers.
A 2012 upgrade closed the centre for 10 months, kept the original roof facade, doubled the seats with rectangular tables, and added new stall exhausts.

history.fact: In the 1970s, mobile stalls and street bazaars were a common sight on Queen Street until hawkers were moved into licensed food centres and markets in the 1980s.

Nearby Albert Street was a popular open-air dining street in the 1970s and early 1980s, and when it was redeveloped in the mid 1980s most of its food stalls moved to a hawker centre at the nearby Albert Complex.
The centre closed in February 2025 for about three months of renovation and reopened on 5 May 2025, brighter and with a lift added for older and disabled visitors.

history.fact: The site was once Rayman Market, a municipal wet market opened in 1952 for the Rayman housing estate.
In 1973 Rayman Market was replaced by Whampoa Market and Food Centre, which was upgraded in 2006 to 2008 and renamed Whampoa Makan Place.
The name Whampoa honours merchant Hoo Ah Kay, nicknamed after his birthplace Huangpu in Guangdong.

history.fact: Singapore's first fish market on this shore opened in 1824 as a timber and atap building, and George Coleman replaced it with an octagonal market in 1838.
Municipal Engineer James MacRitchie rebuilt the market on its present site in 1894, keeping the octagon but adding a clock tower and a cast-iron frame made by Walter MacFarlane & Co in Glasgow.
It was gazetted a national monument on 28 June 1973, taken apart in 1986 to protect it during MRT tunnelling, and reassembled by 1989 before reopening as a festival market.
Unlike NEA's hawker centres it is privately run: its website says it is managed by FairPrice Group's Kopitiam, and Kopitiam carried out a S$4 million renovation in 2013.
